newsitem.title: PERU: Rebels keep hostages Christmas day in Peru siege.
newsitem.headline: Rebels keep hostages Christmas day in Peru siege.

text.p: More than a hundred tired and frightened hostages spent Christmas Day under the guns of Marxist rebels in the Japanese embassy residence, as Peruvians prayed for a softening of their captors' hearts.

While the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels refrained from repeating their "goodwill" releases of previous days, relatives and sympathisers flocked to the siege site hoping to bring the captives some Christmas cheer.

A Catholic priest, Jose Luis Cipriani, entered the residence early on Wednesday to lead the mainly Catholic hostages in prayer following a mass believed to have been given by a Jesuit priest who earlier turned down his chance of freedom.

Throughout this Andean nation, Peruvians prayed for the release of the captives. They staged marches in provincial towns and hoisted flags from their homes. Family members sent seasonal messages over the airwaves to their loved ones.

"Brother, I'm sending you a huge hug ... God bless you, have faith like us, have hope that everything will end well," said Leonor Siura, the sister of captive Peruvian congressman Gilberto Siura, in a radio address.
But there were also signs Peruvians were increasingly impatient that there was no breakthrough in the 8-day-old siege.

"They (the rebels) have already ruined our Christmas and blackened Peru's name on every front page in the world. We shouldn't let them spoil New Year as well," said street-cleaner Cesar Grados, working two blocks from the besieged residence. "The government has to solve this, and fast."

The country was also angered by the surprise release Tuesday of Uruguayan ambassador Tabare Bocalandro following his country's freeing of two alleged MRTA. A move that apparently also annoyed Peru's President Alberto Fujimori, who immediately withdrew his top diplomat from Uruguay.

But the freeing of the Uruguayan ambassador also suggested behind-the-scenes, bilateral negotiations were possible despite the hardline, public stance of Fujimori, who, according to government sources, has reduced his circle of key advisers more than at any other time in his six years of office.
Japanese media covering the siege as it entered its second week hinted that a deal might be near to free the captives by allowing the Cuban-inspired rebels go into political exile in Havana.

But former U.N. secretary-general and leader of the Peruvian opposition political party, Javier Perez de Cuellar, said in an interview published on Wednesday in Paris the guerrillas should be punished.
"A solution without a punishment for the hostage-takers would be difficult to admit," he said.

A local newspaper, Expreso, said on Wednesday Peru's security forces had clear information on the guerrillas inside the residence after they captured a rebel who slipped out of the compound along with a group of 225 hostages released on Sunday.

Peruvian troops were on alert to storm the compound if needed as a last resort but anti-terrorism police sources warned another MRTA unit was established in Lima, ready to strike other targets if the government turned to force.

A restless police force officer, Jonny Rojas, said at the site: "We just want to get in there and blow them (the guerrillas) away. We are tired after doing 12-hour shifts, so imagine how worn out they must be. Now is the time."

In Moscow on Wednesday, Russian President Boris Yeltsin called on members of the Group of Seven nations to help resolve the crisis, perhaps by sending "special anti-terrorist squads from national security services."
The MRTA rebels stormed a fancy reception at the residence on Tuesday night last week, taking prisoner about 500 diplomats and officials from around the world.
Many of those originally held -- including the old, the women, all the American and European hostages -- have been released in what the rebels described as humanitarian gestures.

But the guerrillas were holding on to all the Peruvian government officials, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, the foreign minister and the head of the anti-terrorist police -- to press their demands for the release of jailed comrades.
Six ambassadors from Latin America and Asia, plus around 30 Japanese nationals, were among the remaining hostages.

The hostages got some Christmas comfort when Peruvian police allowed the Red Cross to pump water into residence tanks to enable toilets to function for the first time since the main supply was cut off last week.
Portable lamps were also allowed into the residence to lessen the danger of an accident among the hostages during the nights of captivity, the Red Cross said.
